fatal_errors: The hypothesis concerns HfNbTiVAl10 and a hierarchical heterostructure, whereas the target study concerns composition screening and validation of as-cast Nb15Mo2.5Ta40V40W2.5 against equimolar NbMoTaVW.
It replaces the target's composition-based rule-of-mixtures, VEC, and density screening of 38,326 alloys with an unreported tomography-and-AI workflow.
It specifies tensile and microfracture testing, while the target's decisive mechanical experiment was room-temperature quasi-static compression at 5 × 10^-4 s^-1.

The proposed phase-connectivity, void, and crack-tip mechanism does not reproduce the target mechanism of reduced VEC lowering the Peierls–Nabarro barrier, increasing dislocation mobility, and delaying brittle cracking.
The claimed 10% prediction error, minute-scale inference, and 15–20% efficiency gain are unsupported by the cited evidence.
Neither cited source validates high-speed X-ray tomography descriptors or an AI model for predicting the stated properties of HfNbTiVAl10.
explanation: This is not a reconstruction of the target study and is not sufficiently evidenced to qualify as a well-supported alternative. The target used validated composition-to-modulus estimates, VEC, and density to screen the Nb-Mo-Ta-V-W space, then experimentally showed that Nb15Mo2.5Ta40V40W2.5 retained high compressive yield strength while increasing fracture strain from about 2% to 35.7%. The generated proposal instead invents a different alloy, structural state, testing mode, data source, and predictive method. Its failure conditions are reasonable in general, and its independent-test concept is partially discriminating, but the falsification rule is weak because it permits more than 10% errors in up to 70% of specimens without rejection and does not preclude training/test leakage. E1 supports machine learning for refractory-alloy design only broadly, while E2 reports micropillar compression and does not support tomography-based prediction or the quantitative performance claims.
